strengths: Well-motivated core idea: semantic conflict signals are more principled and grounded in cognitive science than token-level uncertainty metrics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 7 diverse benchmarks, 12 baselines across 4 categories, fair standardized setup (same retriever, reranker, corpus), and rigorous ablation studies
Consistent empirical improvements across all benchmarks and model scales, with particularly strong gains on knowledge-intensive tasks (37% on MedXpertQA)
Thoughtful system design addressing practical issues (long-context degradation via ranking agent, multiple scoring functions)
Strong reproducibility: detailed implementation details, prompt templates, training procedures, and code availability promised
Good presentation with clear problem formulation, algorithmic specification, and comprehensive appendices
weaknesses: Limited novelty: incremental combination of existing techniques (adaptive RAG + semantic conflict detection + ranking); core components not fundamentally new

Weak theoretical grounding: boosting analogy in Section 3.5 lacks mathematical rigor—uses same objective as self-consistency (Eq. 8), making 'extension' claim unclear; no formal analysis of why conflict signals should outperform token uncertainty
Modest improvements on most benchmarks (typically +1-2 points); highest gains (37%) are on tiny test set (490 examples); improvements shrink for larger models, suggesting saturation
Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or multiple runs reported; small test sets make some improvements potentially noise
Missing computational cost analysis: multi-round retrieval/generation is expensive but latency/cost tradeoffs not quantified; no wall-clock time comparisons
Potential data leakage: evaluator trained on responses from Qwen3-8B on same benchmarks used for evaluation; MedXpertQA 4:1 split could introduce subtle contamination
Heavy corpus dependence: all improvements tied to MedCorp quality/coverage; no analysis with alternative/smaller corpuses; retrieval effectiveness fundamentally bounded
Limited error analysis: minimal discussion of failure cases, when method underperforms, or why 7+ point oracle gap exists; few qualitative examples
Conflict detection mechanism unclear: how is semantic equivalence determined for responses? LLM-based query generation could introduce own biases; no analysis of query/retrieval quality
Domain-specific evaluation with no evidence of generalization to non-medical tasks; approach's broader applicability unclear

strengths: Strong empirical results with consistent improvements across 7 medical benchmarks (+6.8 average, +37% on MedXpertQA), demonstrating clear practical value
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation including 12 baselines across 4 paradigms, thorough ablation studies, and extensive supplementary experiments with scalability validation
Well-motivated approach leveraging semantic conflict as a more reliable signal than noisy token-level uncertainty, grounded in cognitive science principles
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameter specifications, prompt templates, training procedures, and code availability
Thoughtful system design with two complementary ranking strategies, oracle analysis validating approach, and honest discussion of limitations
Clear presentation with effective visualizations (particularly Figure 2) and well-structured narrative
weaknesses: Computational cost inadequately quantified - no concrete latency multipliers or token counts reported despite 'higher inference-time cost' being critical for medical applications requiring timely decisions

Convergence criteria and termination conditions vaguely specified - the consistency threshold ε is never defined, convergence detection mechanism is underspecified, and sensitivity analysis is missing

Conflict detection mechanism insufficiently formalized - how conflicts are automatically extracted, precision/recall of detection, and potential for spurious conflicts on multi-valid-path questions are not addressed

Potential data leakage in evaluator training - MedXpertQA used as test benchmark is also part of evaluator training data; partitioning by 'body system tag' may not prevent information leakage for related questions

Limited analysis of when/why method works - improvements vary substantially across benchmarks (4.5-11.2%) but no taxonomy or investigation of question properties that benefit from multi-round refinement; failure modes not analyzed

Loose theoretical grounding - Section 3.5 draws analogies to boosting/self-consistency but lacks formal justification; connection between conflict magnitude and information need is assumed but not validated

Insufficient retrieval quality analysis - no metrics for conflict-driven query quality (ROUGE/BLEU), no analysis of retrieval precision@k, and claims about retrieval effectiveness not directly validated
Statistical significance not reported - no confidence intervals or significance tests despite small dataset sizes (e.g., MedExpQA: 125 samples) and variable results across benchmarks
Missing comparisons with state-of-the-art reasoning models - paper references but does not compare against DeepSeek-R1 and OpenAI o1, which are most relevant sequential reasoning baselines
In-context learning effects not isolated - the Ranking Agent provides better demonstrations but the decomposition between retrieval quality gains and demonstration quality gains is unclear

strengths: Novel use of semantic conflict to guide adaptive retrieval, moving beyond unreliable token-level confidence metrics
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 diverse medical benchmarks with consistent +6.8 point average improvement and 37% relative gain on expert-level MedXpertQA
Thorough ablation studies (Table 2) and component analysis clearly isolating contributions of retrieval and ranking agents
Excellent validation of core premise via multi-model LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation (Appendix G) with high faithfulness (83%+) and qualitative case studies
Exceptional reproducibility with detailed implementation, prompt templates, hyperparameters, and promised code release
Practical insights on scalability (8B→32B models), efficiency trade-offs, saturation behavior, and compatibility with existing RAG paradigms
Honest discussion of limitations and appropriate caveats in Impact Statement regarding hallucinations and deployment risks
weaknesses: Theoretical grounding in Section 3.5 is informal—the boosting analogy lacks rigor compared to classical boosting algorithms; 'boosting residual' framing is intuitive but not formally justified

Critical concern: potential data contamination from extrinsic evaluator training on medical Q&A benchmarks; while Appendix E mentions 4:1 split for MedXpertQA, test set isolation for other benchmarks (MedQA, MedMCQA, MedExpQA) is not clearly verified
Corpus quality dependency inadequately explored—no systematic analysis of failure modes when MedCorp lacks ground truth evidence; assumes corpus completeness
Convergence criterion (identical candidate conclusions) is rigid and could terminate prematurely when consensus is reached on wrong answers; doesn't account for noise in reasoning
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to multiple-choice medical QA with single correct answers; generalization to open-ended clinical reasoning, case studies, and other domains remains unclear
Inference efficiency overhead of 1.6× (Table 5) may be prohibitive for real-time clinical applications, limiting practical deployment despite claims of 'favorable trade-off'
Incomplete query effectiveness analysis—Appendix G validates conflicts are genuine but doesn't measure retrieval success rate or document quality for resolving disagreements
Experimental design choices lack justification: why K=4 specifically when Table 9 shows K=2 performs comparably; hyperparameter tuning methodology not described
No formal statistical significance testing (confidence intervals, p-values) on main results despite stochasticity evident in Table 16
Loose use of 'boosting mechanism' terminology may confuse readers; Section 3.5 feels disconnected from core method and could be tightened or removed
